title: Polynomial-Time Classical Simulation of BosonSampling under Any Constant-Fraction Photon Loss
abstract: Understanding how photon loss changes the classical complexity of BosonSampling is central to assessing the robustness of near-term photonic quantum advantage. In this work, we present a polynomial-time classical simulation algorithm for lossy BosonSampling that applies whenever a constant fraction of the input photons survives. We consider the standard fixed-loss model, where $N$ input photons propagate through an $M$-mode interferometer and exactly $N-n$ photons are lost uniformly at random, leaving $n$ surviving photons at the output. For any constant surviving fraction $n/N\in(0,1)$, the algorithm samples from a distribution within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the fixed-loss BosonSampling distribution with probability at least $1-δ$ over Haar-random interferometers, in time $\operatorname{poly}(M,N,\varepsilon^{-1},δ^{-1})$. We further extend the fixed-loss analysis to the uniform-transmission-loss model and obtain analogous polynomial-time simulability for any fixed transmission rate $η\in(0,1)$. These results substantially extend the known provably simulable regime of $n=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon N})$ surviving photons or $η=O(\sqrt{\varepsilon/N})$ transmission rate, and demonstrate that even the experimentally relevant linear-survival regime can admit efficient classical simulation under the conditions considered here.
summary: This paper provides a theoretical breakthrough by demonstrating that BosonSampling remains classically simulable in polynomial time even when significant photon loss occurs, provided the surviving photon fraction is constant. It analyzes both fixed-loss and transmission-loss scenarios, significantly expanding the boundary of quantum advantage against classical simulation.
main_problem: Assessing the robustness of quantum advantage demonstrated by BosonSampling when subjected to photon loss.
main_result: The authors show that BosonSampling can be classically simulated in polynomial time even when a constant fraction of input photons are lost, extending the known simulable regime significantly.
method: The work develops polynomial-time classical simulation algorithms by analyzing the fixed-loss and uniform-transmission-loss models using techniques involving low-degree approximation and marginal evaluation.
model_or_system: The system is BosonSampling, a process involving $N$ input photons passing through an $M$-mode random interferometer. The analysis considers two loss models: fixed-loss (random loss of $N-n$ photons) and uniform-transmission-loss (independent transmission probability $\eta$).
key_observables: The simulation targets the fixed-loss and uniform-transmission-loss Fock-output distributions, analyzed via collision-collapsed and full Fock-output representations.
important_parameters: The key parameters are the input photon number ($N$), the number of modes ($M$), the surviving fraction ($n/N$), and the approximation error ($\epsilon$) and failure probability ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The main results are established under the dilute-mode condition ($M = \Omega(n^2 N)$) and rely on extending the fixed-loss analysis to the uniform-transmission-loss model by conditioning on the sampled photon number.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the fixed-loss model (a) and the uniform-transmission-loss model (b) for the physical setup.
paper_structure: The paper systematically defines the output representations (Fock-output, collision-collapsed, first-quantized) before presenting the advanced simulation techniques. It then derives error bounds using coloring arguments and concludes with the main theorems establishing polynomial-time simulation for constant surviving fractions.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the feasibility of photonic quantum computation in realistic, lossy experimental settings, which is a major bottleneck for quantum optics and quantum information science.
